ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure is a two-transistor differential amplifier. The collectors of the two transistors are each connected through an R_C to the V_CC above; the two input sources v1 and v2 are applied respectively to the bases of the left and right transistors; the emitters of the two transistors are connected below to the same node, and this common emitter node is then connected through an R_E to -V_EE. Therefore, R_E is the tail/emitter resistor shared by the two transistors, not the emitter resistor independently belonging to each half-circuit. Reasoning: For differential-mode input, v1 and v2 are equal in amplitude and opposite in phase. Since the circuit is left-right symmetric, the common emitter node approximately remains unmoved, so increasing the shared R_E basically has no effect on the ideal differential gain. For common-mode input, v1 and v2 change simultaneously in the same direction, and the common emitter node must also change along with them through R_E; the larger R_E is, the stronger the common-mode emitter negative feedback or degeneration effect is, making the common-mode output smaller. Therefore, a large R_E only reduces common-mode gain, and does not reduce differential-mode gain.

method.method_draft: First identify from the image that RE is the common tail/emitter resistor shared by both transistors, not a separate emitter resistor in each half. Then consider two gain definitions. With differential input, v1 and v2 are equal and opposite; by symmetry the shared emitter node remains nearly fixed, so increasing RE has essentially no effect on differential gain in the ideal amplifier. With common-mode input, v1 and v2 move together; the shared emitter node must move through RE, and a larger RE gives stronger common-emitter degeneration, making the common-mode output smaller. Therefore a large RE decreases only the common-mode gain.

planner_metadata.distinctiveness_rationale: This is the direct small-signal symmetry route: it separates the visually shown differential pair into differential-mode and common-mode excitations and checks where the shared emitter resistor appears. It is the natural single solution for this concept question.
planner_metadata.image_role: Read the circuit as an ideal BJT differential amplifier: two matched transistors with equal collector resistors RC connected to VCC, their emitters tied together at a common node, and that node connected through RE to -VEE; the two base inputs are v1 and v2.
planner_metadata.text_role: Use the question’s phrase “ideal differential amplifier” and its request for the effect of a large RE on the amplifier gains, so the solver must compare differential gain versus common-mode gain rather than compute numeric values.
planner_metadata.knowledge_role: Use differential-pair half-circuit behavior. For differential-mode drive, the common emitter node is a virtual ac ground by symmetry, so the tail resistor RE carries little/no incremental differential signal and does not set the differential gain. For common-mode drive, both emitter currents vary in the same direction, so signal current flows through RE and produces emitter degeneration/negative feedback; increasing RE raises this feedback and reduces common-mode gain.
